primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'stranger' (Hebrew ger, sojourner; Greek xenos) primarily symbolizes the vulnerable outsider in whom God—and specifically Christ—is encountered, so that hospitality to the stranger is treated as a test and expression of covenant faithfulness and love of God. The stranger stands for the marginalized person whom God commands his people to welcome, protect, and love, grounded in Israel's own memory of being strangers in Egypt and culminating in Jesus' identification of himself with the stranger.
primary_basis: Matthew 25:35, 38, 43-44 ('I was a stranger and you welcomed me')
Leviticus 19:33-34 ('love the stranger as yourself, for you were strangers in Egypt')
Exodus 22:21 and 23:9 (do not wrong or oppress a stranger)
Deuteronomy 10:18-19 (God loves the stranger; you shall love the stranger)
Hebrews 13:2 (entertaining strangers, some have entertained angels unawares)
Luke 24:13-35 (the risen Christ unrecognized as a stranger on the Emmaus road)

alternatives.meaning: Believers themselves as 'strangers and pilgrims/exiles' on earth—a symbol of the Christian's true citizenship in heaven and detachment from the present world. This is a very widespread second stream of interpretation, prominent in Puritan, pietist, and pilgrimage theology.
basis: Hebrews 11:13 ('strangers and pilgrims on the earth')
Genesis 23:4 and Psalm 39:12 ('I am a stranger with thee, a sojourner')

alternatives.meaning: The stranger as a symbol of alienation from God and the covenant—those 'strangers to the covenants of promise' who are brought near in Christ; welcome of the outsider then symbolizes Gentile inclusion in the people of God.
basis: Ephesians 2:12, 19 ('no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens')
Isaiah 56:3-7 (the foreigner joined to the LORD)

alternatives.meaning: The stranger as a negative figure: the false shepherd or false teacher whose voice the sheep do not follow, or the 'strange woman' of Proverbs symbolizing temptation, folly, or apostasy.
basis: John 10:5 ('a stranger will they not follow... they know not the voice of strangers')

alternatives.meaning: Christ himself as the divine Stranger—unrecognized, rejected, appearing incognito among his own—a devotional and literary reading built on the Emmaus narrative, Matthew 25, and John 1.
basis: John 1:10-11 ('the world knew him not; his own received him not')

notes: 'Stranger' carries a recognizable but two-sided consensus rather than a single fixed symbol: (1) the outsider to be welcomed, in whom Christ is met (hospitality/love of neighbor), and (2) the believer's own status as a sojourner whose home is heaven. Both are broadly attested across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant teaching; the hospitality/Matthew 25 reading is the most frequently cited in modern preaching and social teaching, while the pilgrim reading dominates in devotional and eschatological contexts. Which is 'primary' depends on tradition and era, so confidence is rated medium. Negative uses (John 10:5; the strange woman of Proverbs) are real but clearly secondary in the interpretive literature.
